notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Acts 19:21–41, using only the pages I was able to read.

**What I couldn't find.** Enduring Word's page cut off before verse 21, so its notes on this section come only from search snippets. I found nothing on these verses from the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal-denominational or prosperity/word-of-faith sites, so I've left those out. The one real split I found (v. 21) doesn't fall along church lines; it divides commentators within the same traditions. Reformed voices (Calvin, the Geneva notes) appear where I found them.

---

**v. 21**
- **Traditional reading:** David Guzik takes "in the Spirit" to mean the Holy Spirit guided Paul's plans. Guided by the Holy Spirit, Paul determined his itinerary. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-19/)
- **The main debate: Holy Spirit or Paul's own spirit?**
  - *Own mind:* Barnes reads it simply as "Resolved in his mind." The Cambridge Bible agrees: he had settled it in his own mind. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-21.htm)
  - *Both:* Ellicott says the Greek implies more than human will, a spirit in communion with the Divine Spirit. Poole says Paul made up his own mind but had the influence and guidance of the Holy Ghost, and that in a more than ordinary manner. (same URL)
  - *Reformed:* Calvin says Paul planned the trip through the instinct and motion of the Spirit; that we may know that all his whole life was framed according to God's will and pleasure. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-21.html) The Geneva notes add that Paul did not rush rashly toward death but as the Spirit of God led him. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-21.htm)
  - *Holy Spirit:* Constable, citing Longenecker, argues the Holy Spirit is at least included. It would be odd to call the Jerusalem trip a human decision while the Rome trip carries the divine "must." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-21.html)
  - *Other options:* Precept Austin lists translations on each side. The NET and NIV take it as Paul's spirit, and Toussaint notes the verb means "purposed," not "was led." Precept Austin concludes the two readings don't rule each other out. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/acts-19-commentary) Matthew Henry gives both options: Paul's own private intention, or the Spirit's direction. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-21.html)
- **"I must see Rome":** Barnes notes He did go to Rome, but he went in chains, as a prisoner. Bengel praises Paul's restless missionary vision. Barnes thinks the main purpose of the trip was the collection for poor believers in Jerusalem. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-21.htm)
- **Modern scholarship (Bible.org, Utley):** It is uncertain which "spirit" is meant. Luke may be showing Paul going to Jerusalem because God led him, not because the riot pushed him out. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21343)

**v. 22**
- Barnes says Paul left once the gospel was firmly established at Ephesus, so that his presence there was no longer necessary. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-21.html)
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) thinks it very unlikely that this Erastus was "the chamberlain of the city" of Corinth. It also says "Asia" here means Ephesus, its chief city. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Act/Act_019.cfm)

**v. 23**
- Guzik notes this is the third time in Acts the movement is called "the Way." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-19/)
- NET note: "the Way" means the Christian movement. Luke's phrase is literally "no little disturbance." (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=Act+19%3A23-41)

**v. 24**
- **What the shrines were:**
  - Ellicott says pilgrims took home silver or bronze models of the sanctuary and the image. He describes the image as unlike Greek art, perhaps a leftover of an older nature-worship like that of Cybele. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-24.htm)
  - The Pulpit Commentary (citing Meyer) says they were carried as charms on journeys and placed in people's houses to ensure to them the protection of the goddess. (https://biblehub.com/acts/19-24.htm)
  - Constable calls Demetrius the leader of the guild. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-24.html)
- **Motives:** Barclay judges the silversmiths cared far more for their own pocketbooks than for Artemis. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-24.html) A sermon on Bible Hub takes a gentler view: Demetrius knew no religion but paganism, and would have helped Paul if the gospel had been good for trade. (https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/19-24.htm)
- **NET notes:** Acts often records the charge that Christianity disrupted the economy or society (16:20–21; 17:6–7; 18:13). The temple was one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=Act+19%3A23-41)

**v. 25**
- NET: In effect, Demetrius gathered the Ephesian chamber of commerce together. Another possible translation is that the trade was "an easy way for us to earn a living." (same NET URL)

**v. 26**
- NET: this one line sums up Paul's attack on idols, like his speech in Athens (17:22–31). "Turned away" can also mean "misled." (NET URL)
- Matthew Henry: the craftsmen couldn't argue against the teaching itself, only against its effect on their country customers. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-37.html)
- Utley (quoted by the Light of Israel commentary) sees the complaint as evidence of how far Paul's ministry had spread across Asia. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)

**v. 27**
- Guzik: Demetrius first appealed to money, then to civic pride. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-19/)
- NET says the issue was not only money: The battle was a "cosmic" one between deities. (NET URL)

**v. 28**
- Ellicott: the tense means they *kept* shouting. The cry was probably the usual chorus of the festivals of Artemis. (https://biblehub.com/acts/19-28.htm)
- Gill: "Diana of the Ephesians" set her apart from many other Dianas. Pausanias names at least sixty. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/acts/19-28.html)
- NET compares the rage to the Jewish crowd's reaction in Acts 7:54. (NET URL)

**v. 29**
- **The theatre:** NET says it held 25,000 and is still standing, which made the event a public spectacle. (NET URL)
- **Which Gaius?** Commentators differ:
  - Smith and the Light of Israel commentary think he was Paul's host in Corinth. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-35.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)
  - Matthew Henry identifies him with Gaius of Derbe (Acts 20:4). His only "crime" was travelling with Paul. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)
  - Light of Israel adds that Aristarchus later joined Paul in his Roman imprisonment (27:2). (same URL)
- MacLaren pictures Gaius and Aristarchus standing silent for two hours, expecting each moment to be their last. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/acts/the-fight-with-wild-beasts-at-ephesus.cfm)

**v. 30**
- NET: the word for "assembly" means the city's formal citizen gathering. (NET URL)
- Matthew Henry: the mob would have treated Paul worse than his companions, seeing him as the ringleader. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)

**v. 31**
- **Who the Asiarchs were:** They were wealthy provincial officials linked to the public games and the cult of the emperor. Coffman sees their friendship as a sign of the gospel's reach into the upper class. Constable: "A sect whose leader had Asiarchs for friends cannot be dangerous to the state." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)
- **Were they converts?**
  - Gill and Barnes: probably not true converts, just well-wishers. (same URL; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-31.htm)
  - Utley: Apparently they had become believers also, or at least friends of Paul. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21343)
  - Ellicott: Paul's tact and courtesy often won respect from officials. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-31.htm)
- **Reformed note:** The Geneva notes urge steadfastness in ministers, but steadfastness that must modestly allow itself to be governed by wisdom. (same URL)
- **NET:** the warning shows how dangerous things had become. (NET URL)

**v. 32**
- Matthew Henry, on the providence in this scene: the town clerk may have been no friend at all to Paul, nor to the gospel he preached, yet his human prudence is made to serve the divine purpose. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)
- Utley (quoted by Light of Israel) points out that the word for this "assembly" (*ekklesia*) is the word later used for "church." (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-34.html)

**v. 33**
- **Why the Jews pushed Alexander forward:**
  - Most think it was to separate the Jews from Paul: Ellicott, Barnes, JFB, the Cambridge Bible, the Pulpit Commentary. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-33.htm) Coffman agrees. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-33.html)
  - Calvin (Reformed) disagrees: the Jews wanted him brought before the people that he might be murdered. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-33.html)
  - Benson and Meyer think Alexander was a Christian thrust out maliciously. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-33.htm)
- **Was he "Alexander the coppersmith" (2 Tim 4:14)?**
  - Clarke and Bengel lean yes. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-33.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-33.htm)
  - JFB says the idea has little support, and the Pulpit Commentary leaves it open. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/19-33.htm)
  - Ellicott (on 1 Timothy) calls the identification unsafe because the name was common. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-timothy/1-20.html)
- **NET:** what his defence would have been is unclear, and he never got to speak. (NET URL)

**v. 34**
- Guzik compares the crowd's chants to modern "Great is my team/party." Yet no one worships Diana today, while millions worship Christ. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-19/)
- MacLaren compares the scene to Baal's priests on Carmel and warns that the voice of the people is not always the voice of God. (MacLaren URL above)
- NET: the uproar shows the racial and social tensions Christians faced in a city like Ephesus. (NET URL)

**v. 35**
- **"Temple guardian":** Henry explains the term (*neokoros*): the city was officially in charge of Diana's worship. He comments that The city was more the patroness and protectress of Diana than Diana was of the city. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-37.html)
- **"Fell from heaven":** NET says many see the image as a meteorite. The phrase supports the goddess's claimed heavenly origin. (NET URL)
- **The clerk's method:** The Contending for the Faith commentary says he calmed the mob like a skilled diplomat, by appealing to their pride. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-35.html)

**v. 36**
- NET: "undeniable" means beyond dispute. The clerk wanted order restored. (NET URL)

**v. 37**
- NET: Paul could be charged with no formal crime. He had a right to his religion as long as he didn't act against the temple. (NET URL)
- Contending for the Faith says much the same. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-37.html)

**vv. 38–39**
- NET: the clerk asks that the courts and the proconsuls be respected. Anything further belongs to a lawful citizens' meeting. (NET URL)

**vv. 40–41**
- NET: the city risked being charged with rioting, since no reason could be given for the disorderly gathering. (NET URL)
- Utley: Luke keeps showing that Christianity was no threat to government. Some think Acts was written for Paul's trial in Rome. (https://bible.org/book/export/html/21343)
- Constable likewise calls the clerk's intervention the best possible defence against the charge that Christianity threatened the empire. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/19-31.html)
